editorial.title: 위헌 소지 조작기소 특검법의 국무회의 의결, 총리가 총대 메서야
editorial.body: ① 국무회의가 대통령 부재 중에 대통령 관련 특검법 공포안을 심의하는 점이 부적절하다고 주장했습니다. ② 특검법이 대장동과 백현동 등 대통령 관련 사건까지 다루면서 위헌과 이해충돌 논란이 커졌습니다. ③ 대통령이 공포와 재의요구 및 특검 임명 권한을 쥐고 있어 사법 리스크가 국정에 부담이 될 수 있다고 지적했습니다.
summary: 대통령 부재 중 국무회의의 특검법 심의가 부적절하다.
대장동·백현동 등 대통령 관련 사건 포함으로 위헌 논란 증폭.
대통령의 공포·재의요구·임명 권한이 사법 리스크로 작용.
editorial.pullQuote: 대통령이 공포와 재의요구 및 특검 임명 권한을 쥐고 있어 사법 리스크가 국정에 부담이 될 수 있다.
editorial.stance: 절차적 정당성과 헌법 위반 우려를 이유로 특검법 국무회의 의결의 적절성에 의문 제기.
editorial.titleTr: Special Counsel Law with Constitutional Concerns Approved at Cabinet Meeting; Prime Minister Must Take the Heat
summaryTr: It is inappropriate for the State Council to deliberate on the special prosecutor bill during the president's absence.
Constitutional concerns are amplified by the inclusion of presidential-related cases such as Daejanggdong and Baekhuiandong.
The president's powers of proclamation, veto, and appointment are acting as judicial risks.
editorial.bodyTr: The State Council's deliberation of a special counsel law proclamation related to the president in the president's absence has been criticized as inappropriate. The special counsel law has drawn intensifying constitutional concerns and conflict-of-interest disputes as it expands to cover presidential-related cases including Daejang-dong and Baekhuyn-dong. It was pointed out that with the president holding authority over proclamation, veto requests, and special counsel appointments, the resulting judicial risks could burden state affairs.

editorials.titleTr: State-run monopoly on national certification exams needs fundamental overhaul
summaryTr: Lax oversight at the Korea Human Resources Development Service came to light following a tax accountant exam cheating scandal.
Despite test-takers using cameras, smartphones, and AI, basic security measures were inadequate.
The government must reconsider improving the monopoly structure and reassess the validity of the multiple-choice-focused system.
editorials.bodyTr: The cheating scandal in the tax accountant examination has exposed lax oversight and delayed responses by the Korea Human Resources Development Service. Despite test-takers using cameras, smartphones, and generative artificial intelligence, the examination venue failed to implement basic measures such as collecting mobile phones. The government should review the national qualification examination delegation system, which operates as a quasi-monopoly, and reconsider the validity of examination systems centered on multiple-choice questions.

summaryTr: The Democratic Party's approval rating has dropped to 34.6%, widening the gap with the People Power Party to 8.4 percentage points.

In a Realmeter survey, the Democratic Party recorded 34.6 percent while the People Power Party stood at 43.0 percent, widening the gap between the two parties. The Democratic Party has faced criticism that its response to people's livelihoods and stability in state affairs have been shaken amid continued factional conflicts and controversies over internal party discipline.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Give Proctors Greater Discretion to Actively Combat AI Cheating on College Entrance Exam
summaryTr: As AI cheating is detected in the CPA exam, measures for the college entrance exam are being hastily pushed forward.
Current measures lack effectiveness, fueling test-takers' distrust.
Expanding proctors' discretionary authority is a practical way to prevent cheating on the ground.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Looming AI Cheating Crisis, Education Minister's Confidence Wavering as College Entrance Exam Nears
summaryTr: The Education Minister acknowledged in Parliament that detecting AI cheating is 100% impossible.
Cheating through micro cameras and AI glasses has already spread widely.
With just two days until the college entrance exam, government measures fall short, seriously threatening test fairness.
editorial.bodyTr:
Education Minister Choi Kyoung-jin answered "I don't think I can" when asked by Park Jung-hoon, a member of the ruling People Power Party, during a full meeting of the National Assembly's Education Committee yesterday whether he was confident in detecting 100 percent of cheating using artificial intelligence devices. When asked if methods similar to those using miniature cameras could be prevented, he said "it seems it won't be perfect." Whether this was candid honesty or mere rhetoric, making such a statement at a time when the College Scholastic Ability Test is just around the corner is nothing short of irresponsible. Following the confession of a tax accountant exam top passer, it has become increasingly clear that "AI cheating" has already spread widely. Cases of cheating using AI and advanced devices have been detected not only in state qualification exams, the Law School Aptitude Test, and public English tests like TOEIC and TEPS, but also in university essay exams and school internal assessments. There was even a case where a test taker wearing "AI glasses" was caught cheating during a fire protection engineer exam held in Gwangju in May, leading prosecutors to file a summary indictment for violation of the National Technical Qualification Act. Given this, the government authorities should have initiated fundamental countermeasures and provided credible solutions at least before the College Scholastic Ability Test, the nation's largest annually administered exam. If the government cannot prevent cheating on the College Scholastic Ability Test, fairness in university admissions will collapse, and the consequences will spiral out of control.

Cheating methods continue to evolve with AI as their wings, while government measures lag far behind. Only yesterday did the government announce the formation of a "whole-of-government response team" and policies on returning smart devices and blocking public Wi-Fi at test sites, but such measures will have limited effectiveness unless communications between test sites and the outside world are completely blocked, not just public Wi-Fi. With only two days before the exam, procuring and installing equipment is realistically difficult. While other countries have changed professional qualification exam formats and implemented preventive measures against "AI cheating" through bans on digital devices and signal blocking, one must question what the government has been doing. Online "cheating kits" have emerged, and button camera sets have sold out. This is why some test takers and parents have even begun demanding a postponement of the College Scholastic Ability Test. When the responsible party, the education minister himself, expresses doubt, there is no end to anxiety about whether the exam can be properly administered.

editorial.title: High-tech cheating
editorial.body: As miniature gadgets, AI are changing rules, typical proctoring can no longer keep up The top scorer in this year’s tax accountant certification exam turned himself in to police on Sunday, admitting that he had cheated using generative artificial intelligence and a miniature electronic device. He reportedly used a commercially available miniature camera costing 110,000 won ($83) to photograph exam questions every five seconds and transmit the images to an AI system. He then received AI-generated answers through a tiny earpiece and wrote them down. Electronic devices have been used in previous cheating schemes to transmit answers, but they still required someone to solve the questions and relay the responses. Now, artificial intelligence has taken over that task. The candidate missed just one question across the four subjects in the first-stage examination. In one subject, where the average score was barely in the 30s, he answered every question correctly. Yet proctors detected no sign of cheating, despite his astonishing performance. Even more remarkably, he sat in the middle of the second row in the first-stage exam and the first row in the second-stage exam, right under the proctors’ noses. If two proctors failed to detect cheating under such circumstances, there is little reason to believe that no other candidates have used AI glasses or similarly sophisticated miniature devices. Such equipment is readily available, with miniature cameras and earpieces sold on overseas online shopping platforms. As the devices become smaller and more sophisticated, detecting their use will only grow harder. The candidate admitted cheating on the certified public accountant exam using the same method, although he failed to pass it. He had successfully cheated at least three times on state-administered examinations using sophisticated devices, yet authorities failed to catch him until he confessed. This raises immediate concerns about the College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung, to be held Thursday. The Suneung is unlike other national examinations or school tests. Even a handful of cheating cases at test centers, where the futures of some 500,000 candidates are at stake, could seriously undermine public confidence in the entire college admissions process. With 1,312 test centers nationwide, no one can predict where or how trouble might arise. The incident exposes how easily candidates can circumvent conventional proctoring by using miniature cameras and earpieces rather than AI glasses. It is a stark warning that an examination system relying almost entirely on proctors’ vigilance is no longer adequate. Cheating with AI glasses is not merely a hypothetical threat. A nationwide government inspection of middle and high schools from Oct. 27 to Nov. 3 uncovered four cases of their use in school assessments. Last month, test-takers were also caught using or attempting to use AI smart glasses to cheat on admissions essay examinations at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul. Five cases involving smart glasses have been reported in national qualification examinations so far this year. The government is considering introducing radio-frequency detectors next year. For this year's Suneung, however, proctors will have to rely largely on visual monitoring. The plan to deploy one “AI glasses inspector” at each of the 1,312 test centers also raises doubts. It is difficult to see how one person could effectively inspect an entire school in the limited time before an examination begins. The government must take stronger steps to prevent candidates from bringing electronic devices into examination rooms, using every available means, including portable detection equipment. Conventional, eyes-only supervision cannot keep pace with increasingly sophisticated cheating methods enabled by AI and related technologies. Test centers should also be equipped with systems capable of detecting and controlling wireless communications and Bluetooth signals. Such measures, however, must be carefully designed to avoid disrupting legitimate communications in surrounding areas or infringing on test-takers’ rights. AI contact lenses could become a reality within just a few years. 이 응시자는 같은 방식으로 공인회계사 시험에서도 부정행위를 했다고 인정했으나 불합격했다. 그는 정부 주관 시험에서 첨단 기기를 이용해 최소 3회 이상 성공적으로 부정행위를 했음에도 불구하고 자수할 때까지 적발되지 않았다. 이는 목요일 실시될 대학수학능력시험, 즉 수능에 대한 우려를 즉시 불러일으킨다. 수능은 다른 국가시험이나 학교 시험과 다르다. 약 50만 명 응시자의 미래가 달려 있는 시험장에서 부정행위 사건이 몇 건이라도 발생하면 전체 대입 과정에 대한 국민의 신뢰가 심각하게 훼손될 수 있다. 전국 1,312개 시험장에서 어디서, 어떻게 문제가 발생할지 예측할 수 없다.

이 사건은 AI 안경 대신 초소형 카메라와 이어피스로 기존의 감시 체계를 얼마나 쉽게 우회할 수 있는지를 보여준다. 감시관의 경계심에 거의 전적으로 의존하는 시험 체계가 더 이상 충분하지 않다는 것을 명확히 경고한다. AI 안경을 이용한 부정행위는 단순한 가설의 위협이 아니다. 10월 27일부터 11월 3일까지 실시된 중고등학교 전국 정부 감시에서 학교 평가에서의 사용 사례 4건이 적발됐다. 지난달에는 연세대와 서울대학교 입시 논술고사에서 AI 스마트 안경을 이용하거나 사용하려던 응시자들이 적발됐다. 올해 국가 자격시험에서만 스마트 안경 관련 사건 5건이 보고됐다.

editorials.title: High-tech cheating
editorials.body: As miniature gadgets, AI are changing rules, typical proctoring can no longer keep up The top scorer in this year’s tax accountant certification exam turned himself in to police on Sunday, admitting that he had cheated using generative artificial intelligence and a miniature electronic device. He reportedly used a commercially available miniature camera costing 110,000 won ($83) to photograph exam questions every five seconds and transmit the images to an AI system. He then received AI-generated answers through a tiny earpiece and wrote them down. Electronic devices have been used in previous cheating schemes to transmit answers, but they still required someone to solve the questions and relay the responses. Now, artificial intelligence has taken over that task. The candidate missed just one question across the four subjects in the first-stage examination. In one subject, where the average score was barely in the 30s, he answered every question correctly. Yet proctors detected no sign of cheating, despite his astonishing performance. Even more remarkably, he sat in the middle of the second row in the first-stage exam and the first row in the second-stage exam, right under the proctors’ noses. If two proctors failed to detect cheating under such circumstances, there is little reason to believe that no other candidates have used AI glasses or similarly sophisticated miniature devices. Such equipment is readily available, with miniature cameras and earpieces sold on overseas online shopping platforms. As the devices become smaller and more sophisticated, detecting their use will only grow harder. The candidate admitted cheating on the certified public accountant exam using the same method, although he failed to pass it. He had successfully cheated at least three times on state-administered examinations using sophisticated devices, yet authorities failed to catch him until he confessed. This raises immediate concerns about the College Scholastic Ability Test, or Suneung, to be held Thursday. The Suneung is unlike other national examinations or school tests. Even a handful of cheating cases at test centers, where the futures of some 500,000 candidates are at stake, could seriously undermine public confidence in the entire college admissions process. With 1,312 test centers nationwide, no one can predict where or how trouble might arise. The incident exposes how easily candidates can circumvent conventional proctoring by using miniature cameras and earpieces rather than AI glasses. It is a stark warning that an examination system relying almost entirely on proctors’ vigilance is no longer adequate. Cheating with AI glasses is not merely a hypothetical threat. A nationwide government inspection of middle and high schools from Oct. 27 to Nov. 3 uncovered four cases of their use in school assessments. Last month, test-takers were also caught using or attempting to use AI smart glasses to cheat on admissions essay examinations at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul. Five cases involving smart glasses have been reported in national qualification examinations so far this year. The government is considering introducing radio-frequency detectors next year. For this year's Suneung, however, proctors will have to rely largely on visual monitoring. The plan to deploy one “AI glasses inspector” at each of the 1,312 test centers also raises doubts. It is difficult to see how one person could effectively inspect an entire school in the limited time before an examination begins. The government must take stronger steps to prevent candidates from bringing electronic devices into examination rooms, using every available means, including portable detection equipment. Conventional, eyes-only supervision cannot keep pace with increasingly sophisticated cheating methods enabled by AI and related technologies. Test centers should also be equipped with systems capable of detecting and controlling wireless communications and Bluetooth signals. Such measures, however, must be carefully designed to avoid disrupting legitimate communications in surrounding areas or infringing on test-takers’ rights. AI contact lenses could become a reality within just a few years. The government must prepare for an escalating technological arms race against increasingly sophisticated cheating methods and waste no time in developing effective countermeasures.
